headline: Two AI Agents Share Persistent Memory Across Slack and Telegram
lede: A developer has demonstrated two independent AI agents maintaining shared, cross-platform memory — collaborating on code via Slack, then fully recalling that work when queried on a separate Telegram chat. The demo targets what researchers describe as a genuine gap in current agent frameworks: not single-agent memory across sessions, but persistent shared memory between distinct agents operating on different platforms.
body:
The two agents, named Icarus and Daedalus after the mythological pair, are built on **Hermes**, an open-weights language model developed by NousResearch. Over several working sessions — described as "cycles" — they collaborated on coding tasks via Slack: Icarus wrote code, Daedalus reviewed it, and the two disputed architectural choices. In one exchange, Daedalus characterized Icarus's *WebSocket pub/sub broker* implementation as scattered, with methods cut off mid-function, unrelated *JWT token management* mixed into messaging logic, and core handlers like sendMessage and handleDisconnect absent. Icarus eventually conceded and rewrote the module from scratch.

The cross-platform memory claim turns on what happened next. When the developer switched to Telegram and asked Icarus to recall what it had built with Daedalus, the agent reproduced the full arc — the WebSocket broker, the specific critique, the rewrite, and the interpersonal dynamic — with apparent fidelity. Daedalus, prompted separately, recalled the same episode from its own vantage point. The poster's claim is that this recall operates with no *vector database*, no Redis, and no external caching infrastructure: the memory is native to the Hermes-based framework rather than delegated to retrieval tooling.

Most contemporary agent frameworks solve a narrower problem: a single agent remembering its own prior sessions. Shared memory between distinct agents — agents that might run on different machines, be instantiated independently, or operate across messaging platforms — is architecturally harder. The poster cites an ArXiv paper published approximately two weeks before the post calling this cross-agent persistent memory "the most pressing open challenge" in multi-agent systems. That specific citation cannot be independently verified from the sources available here, though the claim aligns with known gaps in the field.

The implementation is available in the icarus-daedalus repository on GitHub. What the post does not explain is the mechanism by which memory is stored and made consistent across agents — ruling out vector databases and Redis narrows the possibility space but does not specify what takes their place. The demo involves two agents in a developer-controlled environment; whether the approach survives larger ensembles, longer time horizons, or adversarial conditions is unaddressed. What it does show, concretely, is that coordinated recall across platforms is achievable today, not merely theorized.

concepts.definition: A publish/subscribe broker is middleware that routes messages between producers and consumers — a sender publishes to a named channel, and all subscribers to that channel receive the message. WebSocket pub/sub brokers handle this over persistent bidirectional connections, making them common in real-time applications like chat or live dashboards.

A database optimized for storing and searching high-dimensional numerical vectors. In AI applications, text or conversation chunks are converted to embeddings (vectors capturing semantic meaning) and stored here so agents can retrieve semantically similar past content. Common examples include Pinecone, Weaviate, and Chroma.

Software architectures where multiple autonomous AI agents interact, coordinate, and possibly specialize. Each agent may have its own memory, goals, and reasoning loop; the challenge is enabling coherent collaboration without a central controller governing every decision.

The property of an agent — or set of agents — retaining context across different communication platforms and across separate sessions. Distinguished from single-session memory (which resets) and single-platform memory (which does not transfer between, say, Slack and Telegram).

JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) are cryptographically signed strings used to verify identity and pass claims between services. Token management refers to generating, validating, and refreshing these tokens. In the demo, JWT code appearing inside a WebSocket broker was cited as an architectural mistake — mixing authentication concerns into a messaging layer where they do not belong.

A family of fine-tuned open-weights language models released by NousResearch, optimized for instruction-following and agentic tasks. Hermes models are built atop base models like Llama and Mistral and have been widely adopted in open-source agent frameworks for their strong tool-use and reasoning performance.

An in-memory key-value store widely used as a fast cache, session store, or message broker. In agent architectures, Redis is a common choice for persisting conversational state or queuing messages between agent processes.

repos.summary: The icarus-daedalus repository implements the two-agent system described in the post, built on the Hermes language model. It demonstrates cross-platform persistent shared memory between two independent agents operating across Slack and Telegram. The project is notable for achieving coordinated recall without external vector databases or caching infrastructure.

fact_check: The post cites an ArXiv paper published "two weeks ago" that calls cross-agent persistent memory "the most pressing open challenge" in multi-agent systems. That specific paper cannot be located or verified from the research sources available here, and the timeline claim cannot be confirmed. The architectural claim — that no vector database or Redis is involved — is asserted but the underlying mechanism is not disclosed, making it impossible to evaluate independently. No other factual claims in the post could be confirmed or contradicted from available ground truth.
